Restated before interest: LLY paid $3,152mm of interest inside operating cash flow over 2018 to 2025, 1.17% of revenue. The free cash flow above is struck after it and the valuation already charges the debt by subtracting net debt, so the charge falls by that much, from 28.46% to 27.30%. Restated at replacement capex: LLY spent $23,144mm on plant over 2018 to 2025 against $7,255mm of plant depreciation, 5.89% of revenue above what keeps the plant running. Taken at depreciation, the charge falls from 27.30% to 20.25%. Checked without one-off cash: deal payments are booked under investing, so free cash flow never carried them, and no settlement or transition tax is stated for the window, so the charge stands. Restated without working capital build: over 2018 to 2025 LLY's cash flow statement shows receivables up $15,658mm, inventories up $10,223mm, payables and accrued liabilities up $18,257mm, a working capital build of $7,624mm, 2.83% of revenue. Growth ties that cash up once, not on every product for ever, so the charge falls from 20.25% to 16.87%.

column11: Lilly press release on Kisunla's FDA approval, 2024-07-02 (investor.lilly.com/node/51026/pdf): list price $695.65 a vial, $32,000 for 12 months of therapy
column12: A published annual list price, which the brief puts ahead of the CMS per-beneficiary convention. It is Kisunla's, not remternetug's: Lilly has not priced remternetug. Kisunla is chosen because it is Lilly's own drug against the same target (N3pG amyloid) in the same disease. Judgement: the case against is that a self-injected preventive for asymptomatic people may be priced lower to support wider use, or higher for convenience. The CMS route is not usable here: Kisunla's only CMS year in the book is 2024 at $4,039 a beneficiary, a partial launch year (lookup.py demand Kisunla). The book's other anchor, Leqembi at $27,210 a year from 2025 Part B claims (lookup.py seed Trontinemab), is 15% lower.

column11: CMS ASP pricing file, July 2026 (copy at bms.wv.gov/media/41338/download): J0175 donanemab-azbt payment limit $4.165 per 2 mg. The limit is 106% of ASP (Social Security Act section 1847A), so ASP = $3.929 per 2 mg = $1.9646/mg. Against list of $695.65 / 350 mg = $1.9876/mg, ASP is 98.84% of list, so 1.16% comes off
column12: Direction checked: net is 98.8% of list. Judgement, with a strong case against: this is Kisunla's discount in Part B buy-and-bill. A self-injected subcutaneous product is normally excluded from Part B and sold through Part D and commercial pharmacy benefits, where rebates are larger. Also, if Lilly has raised Kisunla's list price since July 2024 the true gap is wider than 1.16%. The house 0.5 is not applied because it is calibrated to CMS gross spend per beneficiary, not a list price

column12: Expected launch is later. Primary completion is 2029-04 (NCT06653153). Filing is expected in late 2029 and a standard 12-month BLA review would bring approval in late 2030, so the ramp midpoint is shifted instead of the start year, as the book does for trontinemab. Not modelled: TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 1 (NCT05463731), a Phase 3 in early symptomatic AD with an amyloid-clearance primary endpoint, might give an earlier symptomatic launch. It is not in this asset's context and has no sourced readout. Second reader: TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 1 (NCT05463731) has not been shown to have read out its primary endpoint. Topline was guided for March 2026 (BioSpace, Clinical Trials Arena), and search summaries of the registry give a completion date of 2026-05-12, but no topline announcement was found in searches (including Lilly's Q2 2026 release). The only Phase 3 data found is a CTAD 2025 (December 2025) feasibility analysis of self-injection in a 197-patient addendum cohort (NeurologyLive). A symptomatic filing on TRAILRUNNER-ALZ 1 could therefore come well before the preclinical 2030 launch modelled here; that upside is not captured

column11: US residents aged 65+: 61.2mm (Census Bureau Vintage 2024 estimates, census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/older-adults-outnumber-children.html). Less the 7.4mm with Alzheimer's dementia the book carries leaves 53.8mm. Of those, 29.5% are amyloid-positive: 1,323 of 4,486 cognitively unimpaired people aged 65 to 85 screened by amyloid PET for the A4 study (Sperling et al., JAMA Neurology 2020, PubMed 32250387). 53.8mm x 0.295 = 15.87mm; 15.87 / 7.4 = 2.145
column12: Like the trontinemab seed, this scales the book's dementia pool to an absolute label pool. It is above 1 because the trial population, asymptomatic amyloid-positive people, sits outside the dementia pool. Judgement, and probably an overstatement: 61.2mm includes those over 80 (the trial stops at 80) and people with MCI, whom a no-or-minimal-impairment label would exclude. A4 volunteers may also be enriched for amyloid relative to the population. Brookmeyer and Abdalla (Alzheimer's & Dementia 2018) give 46.7mm Americans with preclinical AD, but that counts people from age 30 and includes neurodegeneration without amyloid, so it was not used. If the engine caps eligible_pct at 1.0, set this field null

column10: share of the eligible untreated pool captured per year at peak
column11: The measured anti-amyloid class rate from the book (lookup.py seed Trontinemab): Leqembi's 2025 Part B new starts were 11,396, and Kisunla's Part B beneficiaries went from 1,299 to 9,993, for 20,956 class new starts in 2025. That is 0.954% of the 2,197,800 symptomatic label pool. A 0.5x multiple gives 0.477%
column12: The 0.5x is a judgement. No incumbent treats preclinical AD. Asymptomatic people rarely see a clinician who would test them, and at A4's 29.5% positivity each start needs about 3.4 screens. On a 15.87mm pool, 0.477% is about 75,700 new starts a year at peak, 3.6 times the whole class's 2025 starts. The case for a higher rate: home self-injection removes the infusion-chair and PET bottlenecks, and plasma p-tau217 testing is cheap. The case for a lower one: CMS coverage with evidence development and ARIA MRI monitoring still apply to the class, and payers may resist treating people without symptoms
